learnings.title: The loading waterfall and the critical path
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer: Almost every "make it faster" answer starts in the wrong place — compression, a smaller library, a faster server. The first question is not how big anything is. It is **what the browser could not yet know it needed.** ![The critical path — serialised vs parallelised](/diagrams/sysdesign/loading-waterfall.svg) ## Discovery is the bottleneck A browser can only request what it knows about. Each of these is a *discovery point* — a place where it had to wait to learn the next thing exists: ``` HTML ──▶ finds CSS ──▶ finds @font-face font CSS done ──▶ unblocks render HTML ──▶ finds ``` `defer` for anything your app needs in order; `async` for independent third parties. A bare `

learnings.title: Core Web Vitals — diagnosing and fixing each one
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer: Three metrics, three completely different causes, three different fixes. The interview value is in the **diagnosis** — knowing which measurement tells you which thing is wrong. ## LCP — Largest Contentful Paint When the largest visible element renders. Good: **< 2.5 s at p75.** ### The four parts ``` [ TTFB ] [ resource load delay ] [ resource load time ] [ render delay ] ``` Splitting an LCP number into these four is the entire diagnostic method: | Part | Means | Fix | | --- | --- | --- | | **TTFB** | The server or edge is slow | Cache at the edge, faster origin, streaming | | **Load delay** | The browser discovered the resource late | `preload`, move the URL into the HTML | | **Load time** | The resource is too big | Better format, compression, `srcset` | | **Render delay** | It arrived but could not paint | Render-blocking CSS/JS, or client-side rendering | > "LCP at 4 seconds with a 200 ms TTFB is a critical-path problem. LCP at 4 seconds with a 2.5 second TTFB is a server problem, and nothing I do on the client will help." ### The usual fixes ```html ``` **Never lazy-load the LCP image.** `loading="lazy"` on the hero is one of the most common self-inflicted LCP regressions — it pushes discovery to after layout. ## INP — Interaction to Next Paint The p75 of interaction latency across the visit. Good: **< 200 ms.** Replaced FID in 2024 because FID measured only the *delay before* the first interaction was handled, which was both easy to pass and unrelated to how the page felt. INP measures every interaction, to the next paint. The fixes are the runtime-performance ones: break up long tasks, respond before doing the work, reduce the DOM, avoid layout thrash. See the runtime performance entry. The most common single cause: **a long task somewhere else** was already running when the user clicked. INP is often not the handler's fault at all. ## CLS — Cumulative Layout Shift The sum of unexpected layout shifts. Good: **< 0.1.** A shift counts only if it was **not** within 500 ms of a user interaction — so an accordion opening is fine, and an ad injecting itself is not. ### The five causes, and all five fixes ```css /* 1 · Images without dimensions. The single biggest cause. */ img { aspect-ratio: attr(width) / attr(height); } /* or just set width/height */ /* 2 · Ads, embeds and iframes with no reserved space. */ .ad-slot { min-height: 250px; } /* 3 · Web fonts swapping and reflowing the text. */ @font-face { font-display: optional; /* no swap at all; or use `swap` with a metric-matched fallback */ size-adjust: 105%; /* match the fallback's metrics */ } /* 4 · Content injected above the viewport — a cookie banner, a promo bar. Reserve the space, or overlay instead of pushing. */ /* 5 · Skeletons that are the wrong size. A skeleton must match the real content's height, or it shifts twice: once in, once out. */ ``` **The cookie banner is often the worst offender**, because it is injected late, sits at the top, and pushes everything down at exactly the moment the user starts reading. ## Field versus lab, again | | Lab (Lighthouse, CI) | Field (RUM, CrUX) | | --- | --- | --- | | **INP** | Cannot measure it — there are no interactions | The only real source | | **LCP** | Approximates it | The truth | | **CLS** | Only the shifts during the audit window | The whole session | **Lighthouse cannot measure INP**, and using Total Blocking Time as a proxy in CI is the usual compromise. Say that; it shows you understand what the tools actually do. Use lab to block regressions in CI; use field to decide what to work on. ## A budget that fails the build ```json { "budgets": [{ "resourceSizes": [{ "resourceType": "script", "budget": 170 }], "timings": [ { "metric": "largest-contentful-paint", "budget": 2500 }, { "metric": "total-blocking-time", "budget": 200 } ] }] } ``` A budget that only warns will be ignored. It has to fail. ## Attribution — making the data actionable ```javascript import { onLCP, onINP, onCLS } from 'web-vitals/attribution'; onLCP(({ value, attribution }) => { report({ value, element: attribution.element, // WHICH element was the LCP ttfb: attribution.timeToFirstByte, // the breakdown, for free loadDelay: attribution.resourceLoadDelay, renderDelay: attribution.elementRenderDelay, }); }); ``` The `attribution` build is the difference between "LCP is 3.8 s" and "LCP is 3.8 s, the element is the hero image, and 2.1 s of it is load delay." One is a number; the other is a task. ## Common mistakes - **Averages instead of p75.** Hides the tail, which is the problem. - **`loading="lazy"` on the LCP image.** - **Images without dimensions.** Guaranteed CLS. - **Lab-only measurement.** Cannot see INP at all. - **Optimising LCP without splitting out TTFB.** You may be fixing the wrong half. - **A cookie banner that pushes content.** - **Budgets that warn instead of failing.** ## Key takeaways - Split LCP into TTFB, load delay, load time and render delay before doing anything. - INP replaced FID because it measures every interaction to the next paint; its cause is often a long task elsewhere. - CLS has five causes and all five are fixable by reserving space. - Lighthouse cannot measure INP — use TBT in CI, field data for decisions. - Ship the `web-vitals` attribution build or your RUM is not actionable. ## Interview follow-ups - **"Vitals are green but users complain it's slow."** — Vitals do not measure whether the product works. Add funnel completion, API latency, and a "time to usable" specific to the screen. - **"CLS is 0.3 and you cannot reproduce it."** — It is usually device- or connection-specific: a slow font, a late ad, or a banner. Field attribution names the shifting element. - **"Which do you fix first?"** — Whichever is furthest from its threshold at p75 on your highest-traffic route. Prioritise by traffic, not by which is easiest.

learnings.title: Bundle strategy — splitting, budgets and what actually ships
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
JavaScript is the most expensive thing you ship, because you pay for it twice: once to transfer, and again — usually more — to parse, compile and execute on a device you did not choose.

## The double cost

170 kB compressed is roughly 600 kB parsed. At **~1 ms per KB** on a mid-range Android, that is ~600 ms of main-thread work before anything happens. The transfer was the visible half; the parse is the half that blocks.

That ratio is why "ship less JavaScript" beats every other optimisation, and why a 30 kB image and a 30 kB library are not remotely the same cost.

## Split by change frequency, not by folder

| Chunk | Contains | Changes | Invalidated by a typical deploy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `react.[hash].js` | Framework | Quarterly | No |
| `vendor.[hash].js` | Other deps | Monthly | No |
| `shared.[hash].js` | Your shared UI/utils | Weekly | Sometimes |
| `route-feed.[hash].js` | One route | Daily | Yes |

If your framework shares a chunk with feature code, **every deploy invalidates React for every user**. Split this way and a typical deploy re-downloads 20 kB instead of 700 kB.

## The splits, in order of value

### 1. Route-level — nearly free, biggest win

```javascript
const Feed = lazy(() => import('./routes/Feed'));
const Settings = lazy(() => import('./routes/Settings'));
```

### 2. Heavy, rarely-used dependencies

```javascript
// A chart library, a rich text editor, a map, a PDF viewer — each is
// 150–400 kB and most sessions never open the screen that needs it.
const Editor = lazy(() => import('./Editor'));
```

### 3. Interaction-triggered

```javascript
// Load the editor when the user focuses the box, not on page load.
// Render a cheap facsimile until then.
function CommentBox() {
  const [rich, setRich] = useState(false);
  if (!rich) return <textarea onFocus={() => setRich(true)} />;
  return <Suspense fallback={<textarea />}><RichEditor /></Suspense>;
}
```

### 4. Preload the next likely chunk

```javascript
// On hover or viewport entry, warm the route's chunk so the click
// is instant. Splitting without preloading just moves the wait.
<Link onMouseEnter={() => import('./routes/Feed')} to="/feed" />
```

That last point matters: **code splitting without prefetching trades load time for click latency.** Say both halves.

## Where the weight actually is

Run `source-map-explorer` or `vite-bundle-visualizer` on a real build, and expect these:

| Offender | Fix |
| --- | --- |
| **Moment.js** (~300 kB with locales) | `Intl` or date-fns |
| **Lodash** imported as a whole | `import debounce from 'lodash/debounce'`, or write the four lines |
| **All icons** from an icon set | Import individually, or inline SVGs |
| **Every locale** of a date/i18n library | Load one locale dynamically |
| **Polyfills for browsers you dropped** | Set `browserslist` honestly and use `esbuild` targets |
| **A whole UI kit** for three components | Import per component; check it is tree-shakeable |

**Tree shaking is fragile.** It requires ESM, `sideEffects: false` in `package.json`, and no re-export barrel that defeats it. A `index.ts` that re-exports 80 components is a common and invisible cause of shipping all 80.

## Modern output targets

```javascript
// Shipping ES2015 to browsers that all support ES2022 means shipping
// transpiled generators, async/await helpers and class polyfills for
// nobody. Set the target to what you actually support.
export default {
  build: { target: 'es2022' },
};
```

This routinely removes 10–20% with no code change, and it is the easiest win in the list.

## The budget

```json
{
  "bundlesize": [
    { "path": "dist/assets/index.*.js",  "maxSize": "170 kB" },
    { "path": "dist/assets/vendor.*.js", "maxSize": "120 kB" }
  ]
}
```

> "Bundles don't regress in one bad PR. They grow four kilobytes at a time over six months, and nobody is ever the person who broke it. A hard CI failure plus a size diff comment on every PR makes the cost visible at the moment someone chooses to pay it."

## Measure the right number

Compressed transfer size is what the user downloads; **parsed size** is what blocks the main thread. Report both. A heavily-compressed 40 kB library that expands to 300 kB of code is not a small library.

## Common mistakes

- **Splitting by folder.** Every deploy invalidates everything.
- **Splitting with no prefetch.** Load time becomes click latency.
- **Assuming tree shaking works.** Barrels and `sideEffects` quietly defeat it.
- **Transpiling to ES5 by default.**
- **Measuring only compressed size.**
- **A budget that warns.**
- **Lazy-loading something needed for first paint.** It is now on the critical path, and later.

## Key takeaways

- JS costs twice — transfer, then ~1 ms/KB of parse on a mid-range phone.
- Chunk by change frequency so deploys invalidate as little as possible.
- Route splitting first, then heavy deps, then interaction-triggered — and always prefetch.
- Check the `browserslist` target; it is often free double-digit savings.
- Enforce a budget that fails the build, and surface the diff per PR.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"The bundle is 2 MB. What now?"** — Visualise it first. Do not guess; the answer is usually two or three dependencies, not a thousand small things.
- **"Does HTTP/2 make splitting less important?"** — It removes the request cost, so more chunks are cheap. It does nothing about parse time, which is the expensive half.
- **"When would you NOT code split?"** — A small app where the whole bundle is under budget. Splitting adds requests, complexity, and loading states for no gain.

learnings.title: Images and media — the largest thing you ship
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer: Images are typically 50–70% of page weight and usually the LCP element. They are also where the most bytes can be removed for the least effort — and where the most common CLS bug lives. ## The complete `` Almost every image problem is solved by one correctly-written tag: ```html ``` Each attribute earns its place: | Attribute | Prevents | | --- | --- | | `srcset` + `sizes` | A phone downloading a 1600px image for a 400px slot | | `width` + `height` | Layout shift — the browser reserves the aspect ratio before load | | `loading="lazy"` | Downloading images nobody scrolled to | | `decoding="async"` | Decode blocking the main thread | | `fetchpriority="high"` | The LCP image being deprioritised | | `alt` | An image that is invisible to a screen reader | **`sizes` is the one most often wrong.** It tells the browser how *wide the image will be rendered* — not the viewport width. Get it wrong and `srcset` picks the wrong candidate, which is the same as not having `srcset` at all. ## Format, by what it is | Format | Use | Typical saving vs JPEG | | --- | --- | --- | | **AVIF** | Photos — best compression | 50% | | **WebP** | Photos — universal fallback | 30% | | **SVG** | Icons, logos, anything vector | Usually tiny; inline it | | **JPEG** | Last-resort fallback | — | | **PNG** | Only when lossless is genuinely required | — | ```html ``` ## The two rules that matter most ### 1. Never lazy-load the LCP image ```html ``` `loading="lazy"` on the hero delays its discovery until after layout. It is one of the most common and most damaging LCP regressions, and it is usually introduced by someone applying lazy loading "everywhere" as a blanket optimisation. ### 2. Always reserve the space An image without dimensions collapses to zero height until it loads, then pushes everything down. That is CLS, and it is the single largest source of it on the web. ```css /* Modern browsers derive aspect-ratio from width/height attributes, so setting them is enough — even with responsive CSS sizing. */ img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; } ``` ## Placeholders A blank space is technically not a layout shift and still feels broken. Two good options: - **Dominant colour** — a single hex, effectively free, and enough - **BlurHash / LQIP** — a ~30-byte string decoded into a blurred preview Both go in the API response alongside the URL, so the placeholder is available before the image request even starts. ## Serving A dedicated image CDN (Cloudinary, imgix, Cloudflare Images, or a Next.js image endpoint) is almost always the right answer: ``` /cdn/photo.jpg?w=800&fm=avif&q=75 ``` It negotiates format per browser, resizes on demand, caches at the edge, and means you are not maintaining a build-time resize pipeline. `q=75` is usually visually indistinguishable from `q=100` at a fraction of the size. ## Video - **Never autoplay with sound** — browsers block it and users leave - `preload="metadata"`, never `auto` - A **poster image** is what the user sees first, so it is the LCP element — optimise it like a hero image - Under ~10 seconds with no audio, an animated AVIF or a muted looping video beats a GIF by an order of magnitude. **A GIF is an uncompressed flipbook** and routinely 10× larger than the equivalent video. - Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` for anything decorative ## Accessibility `alt` is not a caption: - **Informative image:** describe what it conveys, not what it depicts. "Revenue rose 40% in Q3", not "a line chart". - **Decorative image:** `alt=""` — an empty string, which tells assistive technology to skip it. Omitting the attribute entirely makes a screen reader read the filename. - **An image inside a link:** the `alt` is the link's accessible name, so it must describe the destination. - **Text in images:** avoid it. It cannot be selected, translated, searched or resized. ## Common mistakes - **`loading="lazy"` on the hero.** - **No `width`/`height`.** The largest CLS source there is. - **A wrong `sizes` value.** Silently disables `srcset`. - **One image for every viewport.** Phones downloading desktop assets. - **GIFs for animation.** - **`preload="auto"` on video.** - **Missing `alt`** rather than `alt=""` for decorative images. ## Key takeaways - One correctly-written `` solves most image problems; `sizes` is the part usually wrong. - AVIF with a WebP fallback; SVG for anything vector. - Never lazy-load the LCP image; always set dimensions. - Ship a placeholder colour or hash in the API response, not as a second request. - `alt=""` for decorative, a meaningful description for informative — and no text inside images. ## Interview follow-ups - **"User-uploaded images of unknown size?"** — An image CDN with on-demand resizing, a hard cap on source dimensions at upload, and store the intrinsic dimensions so the client can reserve space. - **"How do you stop this regressing?"** — A CI check on total image weight per route, plus a lint rule requiring `width`/`height` and `alt` on every ``. - **"How much can this actually save?"** — Typically 40–60% of page weight on an image-heavy page, which is usually more than every JavaScript optimisation combined.

learnings.title: Frontend security — XSS, CSP, CSRF and the supply chain
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
The browser runs on the attacker's machine. Nothing you ship is secret, nothing you validate is trusted, and the code you did not write is most of what runs.

## XSS — still the one that matters

Any attacker-controlled string that becomes executable code.

### The three kinds

| Kind | Vector | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Stored** | Persisted, served to others | A comment containing `<script>` |
| **Reflected** | Echoed from the URL | `?q=<script>` rendered into the page |
| **DOM-based** | Client-side sink, server never involved | `el.innerHTML = location.hash` |

### The sinks

```javascript
// Every one of these turns a string into executable code.
element.innerHTML = untrusted;
element.outerHTML = untrusted;
document.write(untrusted);
eval(untrusted);
new Function(untrusted);
setTimeout(untrusted);              // string form
element.setAttribute('onclick', untrusted);
location.href = untrusted;          // `javascript:` URLs
<a href={untrusted}>                // same
```

React escapes text by default, which removes most of the surface — but `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` puts it straight back. The name is a warning, and it should mean a code review every time.

### The defences, in order

1. **Escape by default.** Let the framework do it. Text interpolation is safe.
2. **Sanitise when HTML is genuinely required**, with a maintained library:

```javascript
import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';
// An allowlist. Never a denylist — you will not think of everything.
element.innerHTML = DOMPurify.sanitize(userHtml, {
  ALLOWED_TAGS: ['b', 'i', 'em', 'strong', 'a', 'p', 'ul', 'li'],
  ALLOWED_ATTR: ['href'],
});
```

3. **Validate URLs by protocol:**

```javascript
// `javascript:` and `data:` in an href are XSS.
function safeHref(url) {
  try {
    const u = new URL(url, location.origin);
    return ['http:', 'https:', 'mailto:'].includes(u.protocol) ? u.href : '#';
  } catch { return '#'; }
}
```

4. **Prefer a structured document model over an HTML string** — see the rich text editor entry. If the stored format has no node type for a script, one cannot exist.

## CSP — the backstop

Content Security Policy assumes something got through and limits what it can do.

```
Content-Security-Policy:
  default-src 'self';
  script-src 'self' 'nonce-{random}' 'strict-dynamic';
  object-src 'none';
  base-uri 'none';
  frame-ancestors 'none';
  report-uri /csp-report
```

- **Nonce-based, not allowlist-based.** Host allowlists are routinely bypassable via JSONP endpoints or hosted user content on an allowed CDN.
- **`'strict-dynamic'`** lets a trusted script load its own dependencies, which is what makes a nonce policy survivable in a real app with a bundler.
- **`object-src 'none'`** and **`base-uri 'none'`** close two commonly-forgotten vectors.
- **Never `'unsafe-inline'` with a nonce** — it silently disables the nonce entirely in browsers that support both.

Roll it out in `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` first and read the reports; a CSP deployed blind takes down the site.

## CSRF

An attacker's page makes the browser send an authenticated request to your API. It works because cookies are attached automatically.

```
Set-Cookie: session=…; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/
```

- **`SameSite=Lax`** covers most cases; it blocks cookies on cross-site POSTs while keeping top-level navigation working.
- **`SameSite=Strict`** is safer and breaks inbound links from other sites.
- **A CSRF token** is still needed for genuine cross-site POSTs and for older browsers.
- **If you use `Authorization: Bearer`, CSRF does not apply** — nothing is sent automatically. That is the one real advantage of token headers over cookies, and it is worth naming.

## Clickjacking

```
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'
X-Frame-Options: DENY
```

`frame-ancestors` is the modern one; ship `X-Frame-Options` as well for old clients.

## The supply chain — the biggest surface

A typical app has hundreds of transitive dependencies. Every one runs with the same privileges as your code, and postinstall scripts run with your build server's privileges.

| Defence | Does |
| --- | --- |
| **Lockfiles, committed** | Pins exact versions including transitives |
| **`npm ci`** in CI | Refuses to resolve anything not in the lock |
| **`--ignore-scripts`** | Blocks postinstall, the classic vector |
| **Subresource Integrity** on CDN scripts | A changed file simply does not execute |
| **Dependabot / audit in CI** | Catches known CVEs |
| **A dependency review habit** | Reject a package with one maintainer and 3 stars for a four-line utility |

```html
<script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.js"
        integrity="sha384-…" crossorigin="anonymous"></script>
```

## Secrets

**There are no secrets in a frontend bundle.** Anything in the JavaScript, in an environment variable baked at build time, or in a network response is readable.

- API keys in the bundle are public keys, and must be scoped and rate-limited accordingly
- Anything that must be secret lives on a server you control, and the client calls it
- Authorisation is server-side. **The client hides the button; the server enforces the rule.**

## Other essentials

- **`rel="noopener noreferrer"`** on `target="_blank"` — otherwise the opened page gets a handle on yours via `window.opener` (modern browsers default to this, but be explicit)
- **`postMessage`**: always check `event.origin` against an allowlist, and never use `'*'` as the target origin for anything sensitive
- **`localStorage` is readable by any script on the page** — never put tokens or PII in it
- **Dependency confusion**: scope internal packages and pin your registry

## Common mistakes

- **`dangerouslySetInnerHTML` on user content** with no sanitiser.
- **Denylist sanitising.** You will miss something.
- **CSP with `'unsafe-inline'`** — usually disables the nonce.
- **Host-allowlist CSP.** Bypassable.
- **No `SameSite`** on session cookies.
- **Tokens in `localStorage`.**
- **Trusting client-side validation** as a control.
- **Believing a build-time env var is secret.**

## Key takeaways

- Escape by default; sanitise with an allowlist only when HTML is genuinely needed.
- A nonce-based CSP with `strict-dynamic` is the backstop; roll it out in report-only mode.
- `SameSite` cookies for CSRF; bearer headers sidestep it entirely.
- The supply chain is the largest surface — lockfiles, `npm ci`, `--ignore-scripts`, SRI.
- Nothing in the bundle is secret, and the server enforces every rule.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"A user pastes HTML into a comment."** — Store a structured document, not HTML. If it must be HTML, DOMPurify with an allowlist, plus CSP as the backstop.
- **"Where do you put the auth token?"** — `httpOnly` `SameSite` cookie, or in memory with a refresh cookie. Never `localStorage`.
- **"How would you audit this?"** — CSP in report-only, `npm audit` and a dependency review in CI, a grep for every XSS sink, and a check that authorisation is enforced server-side.

learnings.title: Internationalisation — bundles, RTL, plurals and dates
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
Cheap to design in, brutal to retrofit — which is exactly why it belongs in the architecture stage even when the product currently ships in one language. ## Never concatenate strings ```javascript // Broken in every language whose word order differs from English, // which is most of them. `Deleted ${count} ${count === 1 ? 'item' : 'items'} from ${folder}`; // ICU MessageFormat: the translator controls the whole sentence, // including where the variables go and what the plural rules are. t('deleted', { count, folder }); // en: "Deleted {count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}} from {folder}" // pl: "Usunięto {count, plural, one {# element} few {# elementy} // other {# elementów}} z {folder}" ``` **Pluralisation is not `n === 1`.** Polish has three forms, Arabic six, Japanese one. ICU encodes each language's actual rules; a ternary encodes English's. Equally: **never build a sentence from fragments.** `"Showing " + n + " of " + total` gives translators three disconnected pieces and no way to reorder them. ## Bundles and loading ```javascript // Ship one locale, not forty. const messages = await import(`./locales/${locale}.json`); ``` - **Resolve the locale server-side** from the URL, a cookie, or `Accept-Language` — then server-render in it, so there is no flash of English. - **Split by route as well as by locale** for large apps; a settings page's strings need not load with the feed. - Keep a **fallback chain**: `pt-BR → pt → en`, so a missing key degrades rather than rendering `settings.profile.title`. **Never render a raw key when a translation is missing.** In development, warn loudly; in production, fall back down the chain. ## RTL is layout, not a stylesheet ```css /* Logical properties flip automatically with `dir`. */ margin-inline-start: 16px; /* not margin-left */ padding-inline-end: 8px; /* not padding-right */ border-inline-start: 2px; /* not border-left */ text-align: start; /* not left */ inset-inline-start: 0; /* not left: 0 */ ``` Set `dir="rtl"` on `` and logical properties handle the layout. Then the parts that do not flip automatically: | Element | Behaviour in RTL | | --- | --- | | **Icons with direction** (arrows, back, next) | Mirror | | **Icons without** (play, clock, checkmark, logos) | Do **not** mirror | | **Numbers and phone numbers** | Stay LTR | | **Code and URLs** | Stay LTR | | **`transform: translateX`** | Does **not** flip — you must handle it | | **Shadows and gradients** | Often need mirroring by hand | A play button that mirrors in Arabic is the classic tell that someone applied `transform: scaleX(-1)` to everything. ## `Intl` for everything formattable ```javascript new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: 'currency', currency: 'JPY' }).format(1234); // ¥1,234 — and Japanese yen has no decimal places, which Intl knows new Intl.DateTimeFormat(locale, { dateStyle: 'long' }).format(date); // 12 September 2026 / 12. September 2026 / 2026年9月12日 new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat(locale, { numeric: 'auto' }).format(-1, 'day'); // "yesterday" — not "1 day ago" new Intl.ListFormat(locale, { type: 'conjunction' }).format(['a', 'b', 'c']); // "a, b, and c" — the Oxford comma is locale-dependent new Intl.Collator(locale).compare(a, b); // Sorting. "ä" sorts differently in German and Swedish. ``` `Intl.Collator` is the one people miss: `Array.sort()` on strings uses code-point order, which is wrong in every language with accented characters. ## Text expansion German runs 30–40% longer than English; Finnish more. Russian and Greek expand too. - **Never fix a button's width** to its English label - Test with a **pseudo-locale** — `[Ŝéţţîñĝŝ ~~~~]` — which catches truncation, hard-coded strings, and concatenation all at once, without waiting for real translations - Allow two-line buttons, or use `text-overflow: ellipsis` with a `title` ## The things that are not strings Localisation is more than text: - **Date order** — `01/02/2026` is ambiguous; prefer a written month in anything consequential - **Number separators** — `1,234.56` vs `1.234,56` - **Week start** — Sunday, Monday or Saturday, by locale - **Name order** — family name first in much of East Asia; a single `fullName` field is safer than assuming first/last - **Address formats** — do not require a US-shaped address globally - **Currency** — the symbol, its position, and the number of decimal places all vary - **Images and colour** — can carry meaning that does not travel ## Accessibility overlap ```html

… Interview Kit …

``` `lang` is what tells a screen reader which voice and pronunciation rules to use. A page with the wrong `lang` is read in the wrong accent and is often unintelligible. Mark inline language changes too. ## Common mistakes - **String concatenation** instead of ICU messages. - **`n === 1` pluralisation.** - **Physical CSS properties** (`margin-left`) instead of logical ones. - **Mirroring every icon** in RTL. - **`Array.sort()` on user-visible strings.** - **Shipping every locale's bundle.** - **Rendering the raw key on a missing translation.** - **Fixed-width buttons** sized to English. - **Missing or wrong `lang`.** ## Key takeaways - ICU MessageFormat, never concatenation — the translator owns the whole sentence. - Logical CSS properties do most of RTL; icons and transforms are the exceptions. - `Intl` for numbers, dates, relative times, lists and collation. - Load one locale, resolved server-side, with a fallback chain. - Pseudo-locale testing finds expansion and hard-coded strings before translators do. ## Interview follow-ups - **"How do you stop hard-coded strings creeping in?"** — A lint rule that flags string literals in JSX, plus pseudo-locale in a staging environment where untranslated text is obvious. - **"User-generated content in mixed directions?"** — `dir="auto"` on the element lets the browser infer direction from the first strong character. - **"How much does this cost if we add it later?"** — Every string, every layout, and every date in the codebase. It is the definition of a change that is cheap up front and expensive later.

learnings.title: Error handling, retries and graceful degradation
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
The happy path is the easy half. What separates a design that survives contact with a real network is having decided, in advance, what each kind of failure looks like to the user.

## Classify the failure first

Different failures need opposite responses, and treating them identically is the root mistake:

| Class | Example | Retry? | Show |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Transient network** | Timeout, connection reset, 502/503 | **Yes**, with backoff | "Reconnecting…", keep existing data |
| **Rate limited** | 429 | Yes, honour `Retry-After` | "Too many requests, retrying in 30s" |
| **Client error** | 400, 422 | **No** — it will fail identically | The specific field errors |
| **Auth** | 401 | Refresh once, then no | Re-authenticate |
| **Forbidden** | 403 | No | "You don't have access", not a retry |
| **Not found** | 404 | No | An empty state, not an error |
| **Server bug** | 500 | Once, cautiously | "Something went wrong", plus a report id |

**Retrying a 400 is the most common retry bug.** It cannot succeed, and you have tripled the load and the latency for nothing.

## Retry with backoff and jitter

```javascript
async function withRetry(fn, { attempts = 3 } = {}) {
  for (let i = 0; i < attempts; i += 1) {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } catch (err) {
      if (!isRetryable(err) || i === attempts - 1) throw err;
      // Jitter is not optional. Without it, every client that failed
      // during an outage retries at the same instant and re-kills the
      // service the moment it recovers.
      const base = Math.min(30_000, 2 ** i * 500);
      await sleep(base * (0.5 + Math.random()));
    }
  }
}
```

**Only retry idempotent operations.** A retried GET is free; a retried POST without an idempotency key creates a second order. Every mutation that might be retried needs a client-generated key.

## The circuit breaker

After repeated failures, stop trying for a while. It protects the recovering service and gives the user a faster, more honest answer than a spinner that will time out.

```javascript
// closed → (failures) → open → (cooldown) → half-open → closed | open
if (state === 'open' && Date.now() < openUntil) {
  throw new ServiceUnavailable('Recommendations are unavailable');
}
```

## Error boundaries decide the blast radius

Where you place them is an architectural decision — it determines whether a bug degrades one panel or blanks the page.

```javascript
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<FeedFailed onRetry={refetch} />}>
  <Feed />
</ErrorBoundary>
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<RecommendationsUnavailable />}>
  <Recommendations />   {/* nice to have — must never take the page down */}
</ErrorBoundary>
```

One boundary at the root means any bug anywhere blanks the app. One per major region means a broken recommendations widget is a small empty card.

**What boundaries do not catch**, and you must handle separately:

```javascript
window.addEventListener('error', report);              // sync errors outside React
window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', report); // rejected promises
// Event handlers: try/catch or a wrapper — boundaries never see these.
```

## Degradation, designed

For each dependency, decide in advance what the product does without it:

| Dependency | Degrades to |
| --- | --- |
| Recommendations | Hide the section entirely — no error, no empty box |
| Live prices | Last known value, clearly marked stale, with a timestamp |
| Search | The plain list with client-side filtering |
| Analytics | Nothing visible — it must never break the page |
| Images CDN | The placeholder colour, and the layout holds |
| Feature flag service | The **safe default**, cached from the last successful fetch |

That last one matters: a flag service returning nothing must not disable your product. Cache the last known values and fail to a defined default.

> "For each third party I'd write down what happens when it's down. Recommendations vanish silently. The price shows its last value with a timestamp. Analytics failing is invisible. None of those need an error dialog."

## The four states, every time

Every screen that fetches has four states, and "I forgot the empty state" is a real deduction:

| State | Design |
| --- | --- |
| **Loading** | A skeleton at the real size, so nothing shifts |
| **Empty** | Why it is empty, and what to do — never a blank area |
| **Error** | What happened, what to do, and **keep any data already on screen** |
| **Success** | The content |

**Never blank the screen on a refetch failure.** If page 1 loaded and page 2 failed, show page 1 plus a retry. Replacing good data with an error message is a strictly worse outcome than the failure itself.

## Error messages people can act on

```javascript
// Useless.
'An error occurred'

// Actionable: what happened, what they can do, and a reference.
'Could not save your changes — your connection dropped.
 We saved a local copy and will retry automatically.
 If it keeps happening, quote reference 8f3a2b.'
```

Include a **correlation id** that also appears in your error tracking. It turns an unreproducible support ticket into a single search.

## Offline

```javascript
// `navigator.onLine` means "has a network interface", not "the
// internet works". Captive portals and dead wifi both report true.
// A failed request is the real signal.
window.addEventListener('offline', () => setConnection('offline'));
window.addEventListener('online', () => { setConnection('online'); flushOutbox(); });
```

Treat `navigator.onLine === false` as definitive (you are certainly offline) and `true` as a hint only.

## Common mistakes

- **Retrying non-idempotent requests** without an idempotency key.
- **Retrying 4xx.** Cannot succeed.
- **Backoff without jitter.** Synchronised retry storms.
- **One root error boundary.**
- **Blanking the screen on a refetch failure.**
- **No empty state.**
- **`navigator.onLine` trusted as truth.**
- **Error messages with no action and no reference.**

## Key takeaways

- Classify the failure before deciding anything; retry only what can succeed.
- Exponential backoff with jitter, and idempotency keys on every retryable mutation.
- Error boundaries per region define the blast radius; they miss handlers and async.
- Write down the degraded behaviour for every dependency, in advance.
- Four states always, and never replace good data with an error.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"The API is down for ten minutes."** — Cached reads stay visible and marked stale, writes queue in a durable outbox, the circuit breaker stops hammering, and one honest banner explains it.
- **"How do you test failure paths?"** — Mock every status code, throttle and fail requests in DevTools, and use a chaos mode in staging that fails a percentage of calls.
- **"A third party is slow, not down."** — Worse than down. Time out aggressively and degrade; a slow dependency you keep waiting on becomes your latency.

learnings.title: Testing strategy for a large frontend
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
A design round question far more often than people expect, because "how do you know it works" and "how does a team of thirty ship on Friday" are the same question.

## The shape: a trophy, not a pyramid

The classic pyramid — mostly unit tests — is a poor fit for frontends, where most bugs live in *integration*: a component wired to a store wired to a fetch.

```
        ╱ e2e ╲              few, slow, highest confidence
      ╱─────────╲
    ╱ integration ╲          MOST of your tests — the widest layer
  ╱───────────────╲
 ╱   unit    ╲                pure logic only
╱──────────────╲
   static (types, lint)       free, runs on every keystroke
```

**Integration is the widest layer.** A test that renders a component with a mocked network and asserts what the user sees catches the bugs that actually ship, and does not break when you rename an internal variable.

## Test behaviour, not implementation

```javascript
// Brittle: breaks when you rename state or restructure the component,
// and passes when the button is broken for a keyboard user.
expect(wrapper.state('isOpen')).toBe(true);

// Durable: describes what a user experiences.
await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Delete project' }));
expect(await screen.findByRole('dialog', { name: 'Delete project?' })).toBeVisible();
```

**Query by role and accessible name.** It is a better test *and* it is an accessibility assertion: if `getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })` cannot find your control, a screen reader user cannot either. That dual purpose is the strongest argument for Testing Library's query priority, and worth saying out loud.

## Mock the network, not your modules

```javascript
// MSW intercepts at the network layer, so the component's own
// fetch/axios/React Query code all really runs.
const server = setupServer(
  http.get('/api/feed', () => HttpResponse.json({ items: [...] })),
);

// And the failure paths, which are the ones that regress.
server.use(http.get('/api/feed', () => HttpResponse.error()));
```

Mocking your own data layer means the thing most likely to be broken — the wiring between the component and the network — is the one thing never exercised.

## What each layer is for

| Layer | Tests | Keep it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Types + lint** | Contracts, obvious mistakes | Free, in the editor |
| **Unit** | Pure functions — formatters, reducers, algorithms | Fast, plentiful, cheap |
| **Integration** | A feature with a mocked network | The bulk of the suite |
| **E2E** | A handful of critical journeys | Signup, checkout, the core loop |
| **Visual regression** | Design system components | Catches what assertions cannot |
| **Contract** | The API shape your client expects | Catches backend drift before production |
| **Accessibility** | axe on every rendered tree | One line in the integration tests |

### E2E: few, and only the ones that matter

E2E tests are slow, flaky and expensive to maintain. Ten good ones beat two hundred.

```javascript
// Signup, checkout, and the single thing the product exists to do.
test('a user can complete checkout', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/product/42');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Checkout' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('Order confirmed')).toBeVisible();
});
```

Kill flaky tests immediately. A suite people re-run until it goes green is worse than no suite, because it trains the team to ignore red.

### Contract tests catch the class nothing else does

The frontend mocks `{ id, name }`. The backend ships `{ id, fullName }`. Every frontend test passes; production breaks. A contract test — Pact, or a shared schema validated on both sides — is the only layer that catches this.

## Accessibility in the suite

```javascript
it('has no axe violations', async () => {
  const { container } = render(<Checkout />);
  expect(await axe(container)).toHaveNoViolations();
});
```

Cheap, automatic, and catches ~30–40% of issues. The rest needs a keyboard walkthrough and a screen reader — automated coverage is a floor, not a pass.

## Determinism

Flakiness comes from a short list of causes, and all are fixable:

- **Time** — inject a clock or use fake timers; never `new Date()` inside logic under test
- **Randomness** — inject the generator
- **Network** — always mocked in integration; retried-but-stubbed in e2e
- **Animations** — disable them in the test environment
- **Arbitrary waits** — `await waitFor(assertion)`, never `sleep(500)`
- **Test order** — reset all state between tests; a test that only passes second is a bug

## What not to test

- **Implementation details** — internal state, private methods, render counts
- **Third-party libraries** — React's rendering is React's problem
- **Chasing 100% coverage** — it produces tests written to hit lines, and a high number that means nothing. Cover the paths that matter, and know which those are.
- **Snapshot tests of large trees** — they fail on every change and get regenerated without being read, which is worse than having no test

## CI shape

```
On every PR:  types → lint → unit + integration → build → bundle budget
              ~3–5 minutes, blocking

On merge:     e2e on a preview deploy → visual regression
              ~10 minutes, blocking the deploy

Nightly:      full cross-browser matrix, Lighthouse, a11y sweep
```

**Keep the PR loop under five minutes.** Beyond that, people stop waiting and start merging hopefully.

## Common mistakes

- **A pyramid with mostly unit tests.** Misses the integration bugs that actually ship.
- **Testing internal state.** Brittle and misses real breakage.
- **Mocking your own data layer** instead of the network.
- **Too many e2e tests.** Slow and flaky, and eventually ignored.
- **Tolerating flakes.**
- **Coverage as a goal.**
- **`sleep()` instead of `waitFor`.**
- **No contract test**, so backend drift reaches production.

## Key takeaways

- Testing trophy: integration is the widest layer for frontend work.
- Query by role and accessible name — a better test and an a11y assertion at once.
- Mock at the network boundary so your real data code runs.
- Few, high-value e2e tests; contract tests for the backend boundary.
- Determinism is a design property: inject time, randomness and network.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"A flaky test in CI. What do you do?"** — Quarantine it immediately so it stops eroding trust, then fix or delete it. Never re-run until green.
- **"How do you test something that depends on time?"** — Inject a clock. It makes the code better and the test deterministic.
- **"How do you test a component nobody can describe?"** — That is a design problem. If you cannot state what a user should experience, there is nothing to assert.

learnings.title: Feature flags and progressive rollout
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
The mechanism that decouples **deploy** from **release** — and, not incidentally, the cheapest alternative to most of the reasons people reach for micro-frontends.

## Deploy is not release

```
Deploy  = the code is on the servers
Release = users can see it
```

Separating them changes how a team works: merge to main continuously, deploy many times a day, and turn a feature on when it is ready — for 1% first, then 10%, then everyone. No long-lived branches, no merge hell, no big-bang launch.

> "Feature flags give you independent release without independent deployment, and that's what most teams actually want when they ask for micro-frontends."

## Four kinds, with different lifetimes

Conflating them is what produces a codebase with forty permanent branches:

| Kind | Lives | Owner | Removed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Release toggle** | Days to weeks | The team shipping it | **Immediately after 100%** |
| **Experiment** | The length of the test | Product / data | When the result is called |
| **Ops kill switch** | Forever | The on-call rota | Never — it is infrastructure |
| **Entitlement** | Forever | Product | Never — it is a pricing feature |

**Only the first two are technical debt.** Every release toggle needs an owner and an expiry date at the moment it is created, or nobody will ever dare delete it.

## Evaluation — where and when

```javascript
// Evaluate on the SERVER for anything that affects first paint.
// A client-side flag means rendering variant A, then flipping to B —
// a visible flash and a layout shift.
const flags = await evaluateFlags({ userId, attributes });
return <App initialFlags={flags} />;
```

For client-evaluated flags, **bootstrap the payload into the HTML** rather than fetching it — a flag fetch on load is a request on the critical path that gates your whole UI.

**Consistent bucketing** matters as much as the split:

```javascript
// Hash the stable user id, not a random number. The same user must
// get the same variant on every visit and on every device, or your
// experiment measures noise and your users see the UI change randomly.
const bucket = hash(`${flagKey}:${userId}`) % 100;
const enabled = bucket < rolloutPercentage;
```

## Failing safe

The flag service is a dependency, and it will be unavailable at some point:

```javascript
// A flag service that is down must NEVER disable your product.
const flags = {
  ...DEFAULTS,            // compiled-in safe defaults
  ...cachedFlags,         // last successful fetch, from localStorage
  ...(await fetchFlags().catch(() => ({}))),
};
```

Three layers: compiled-in defaults, a cached last-known-good, then the live value. The default for a release toggle is **off**; for a kill switch it is **on** (the feature works) so a flag outage does not take down a working product.

## Progressive rollout

```
1%  → watch errors and vitals for an hour
10% → watch for a day
50% → watch for a day
100% → then DELETE the flag and the old code path
```

Automate the guardrails: if the error rate or p75 LCP for the flagged cohort regresses beyond a threshold, roll back automatically. A rollout nobody is watching is just a slower deploy.

## Keeping the code honest

```javascript
// Good: the branch is at the boundary, both paths are whole.
{flags.newCheckout ? <CheckoutV2 /> : <CheckoutV1 />}

// Bad: the flag threaded through the internals. Neither path is
// readable, and deleting the flag is now a refactor.
<Checkout showNewSummary={flags.a} useNewValidation={flags.b} />
```

**Branch at the highest sensible boundary.** It keeps both paths comprehensible and makes removal a deletion rather than an untangling.

### Testing with flags

You cannot test 2^n combinations. Test the paths that will actually exist:

- Every flag **off** (current production)
- Every release flag **on** (the near future)
- Each flag on individually
- Any pair with a known interaction

And put a lint rule or CI check on flag age, so a toggle older than 90 days fails the build with the name of its owner.

## Experiments

- **One metric decided before you start**, or you will find something significant by accident
- **Do not peek** — stopping as soon as it looks good is how you ship a coin flip
- **Guard rails**: an experiment that improves clicks and worsens LCP or error rate is not a win
- **Consistent bucketing** across sessions and devices, or you are measuring noise

## Common mistakes

- **Flags with no owner or expiry.** Permanent branching.
- **Client-side evaluation** for anything above the fold. Flash of the wrong variant.
- **Random bucketing.** Users see the UI change between visits.
- **A flag outage that breaks the product.**
- **Flags threaded through internals.** Removal becomes a refactor.
- **Rolling out with no automated guardrail.**
- **Peeking at experiment results.**

## Key takeaways

- Flags separate deploy from release, which is what most "we need micro-frontends" requests really want.
- Four kinds with different lifetimes; only release toggles and experiments are debt.
- Evaluate server-side for anything affecting first paint; bootstrap the payload.
- Bucket on a stable hashed user id so variants are consistent.
- Fail safe through compiled defaults and a cached last-known-good, and delete the flag at 100%.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"How do you stop flags accumulating?"** — An owner and expiry at creation, a CI check on age, and making deletion part of the rollout ticket rather than a follow-up nobody schedules.
- **"A flag needs to change instantly during an incident."** — That is a kill switch: short TTL or a push channel, evaluated server-side, with no build step in the path.
- **"How do flags interact with caching?"** — The flag becomes part of the cache key, or you cache a variant and serve it to the wrong cohort. This is the bug that turns a 5% rollout into 100%.

learnings.title: Scaling the codebase — monorepo, ownership and guardrails
learnings.source: user request: frontend system design curriculum
learnings.answer:
The Staff-level topic: an architecture that does not fit the organisation does not survive contact with it. Most large-codebase problems are coordination problems wearing technical clothes.

## Monorepo or polyrepo

| | Monorepo | Polyrepo |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Atomic cross-package change** | One PR | N PRs, coordinated, in order |
| **Shared dependency versions** | One, enforced | Drift, immediately |
| **Discoverability** | Everything is there | Requires knowing where to look |
| **CI cost** | Needs affected-only builds or it crawls | Naturally scoped |
| **Independent release** | Needs tooling | Free |
| **Tooling investment** | Real and ongoing | Minimal |

**Monorepo is the default for a product org**, because the dominant cost in a growing frontend is changing a shared component and updating every consumer. Polyrepo makes that a multi-day coordination exercise; a monorepo makes it one reviewable diff.

The cost is real: without affected-only CI (Nx, Turborepo, Bazel), a 40-package monorepo runs every test on every PR and becomes unusable.

## Ownership is the actual architecture

```
# CODEOWNERS
/packages/design-system/   @org/design-systems
/apps/checkout/            @org/payments
/packages/api-client/      @org/platform
```

Boundaries only exist if they are enforced. Two mechanisms, and you want both:

```javascript
// 1 · Lint the import graph. A feature importing another feature's
//     internals is the beginning of a big ball of mud.
'import/no-restricted-paths': ['error', {
  zones: [
    { target: './src/features/checkout', from: './src/features/feed' },
    { target: './src/features', from: './src/app' },
  ],
}]
```

```javascript
// 2 · Only the package's public entry point is importable.
// package.json
{ "exports": { ".": "./src/index.ts" } }   // no deep imports
```

Without these, "modules" are a naming convention, and in eighteen months every module imports every other one.

## The dependency direction rule

One rule prevents most architectural rot:

```
apps  →  features  →  shared/ui  →  shared/utils
```

Dependencies point **one way only**. `shared/ui` must never import from a feature; two features must never import each other. If two features need the same thing, it moves down into `shared`.

A circular dependency between features is the signal that the boundary is in the wrong place.

## Guardrails that scale better than review

At thirty engineers, code review cannot hold the line on things a machine can check:

| Guardrail | Prevents |
| --- | --- |
| **Bundle budget, failing** | Death by 4 kB per PR |
| **Import boundary lint** | Cross-feature coupling |
| **Dependency allowlist** | A second date library, a second state library |
| **`CODEOWNERS` review required** | Changes to shared code landing unnoticed |
| **Visual regression on the design system** | A padding change breaking 60 screens |
| **Lighthouse budget in CI** | Silent performance regression |
| **Flag age check** | Permanent branching |
| **Generated API types** | Client and server drifting |

> "I'd make the rules mechanical wherever I can. A convention in a wiki lasts about one quarter; a lint rule lasts until someone deliberately changes it, and that change is a conversation with a diff."

## Shared code needs a versioning contract

- **Semver, taken seriously** — a visual change that breaks layouts is breaking even if the types did not move
- **Deprecate before removing**, with a dev-time warning for at least one minor version
- **Ship a codemod** for every breaking change; migrating 200 call sites by hand is how a version gets stranded
- **Track usage**, so you know what can be removed and who to tell

## Onboarding is an architectural property

A design that a new engineer cannot navigate has a permanent tax:

- **A predictable structure** — same shape in every feature folder
- **One way to do each thing.** Three state libraries means every new engineer learns three.
- **Templates or generators** for a new feature, so the right shape is the easy shape
- **A README per package** saying what it owns and what it must not depend on
- **An architecture decision record** for choices that will otherwise be re-litigated every six months

A useful test to state out loud: **can a new engineer ship a small change safely in their first week?** If not, the problem is structural.

## When to split the repo

Genuine reasons, not aesthetic ones:

- CI is unavoidably slow even with affected-only builds
- A package is consumed by genuinely external parties
- Legal or compliance boundaries require separation
- Deploy coupling is the *measured* bottleneck, and flags have not solved it

Note the order: **try flags and trunk-based development before splitting anything.**

## Common mistakes

- **Boundaries by folder name only.** Not enforced, so not real.
- **Circular feature dependencies.**
- **A monorepo with no affected-only CI.** Unusably slow.
- **Multiple libraries for the same job.**
- **Conventions in a wiki** instead of in lint.
- **Breaking changes with no codemod.**
- **Micro-frontends adopted for modularity**, which a monorepo gives you free.

## Key takeaways

- Monorepo by default for a product org; the cost is affected-only CI tooling.
- Ownership plus an enforced import graph is the real architecture.
- Dependencies point one way; a cycle means the boundary is wrong.
- Make rules mechanical — a lint rule outlives a convention.
- Onboarding time is an architectural metric, not a documentation problem.

## Interview follow-ups

- **"CI takes 40 minutes."** — Affected-only builds, remote caching, parallelism, and move the slow checks off the PR path to post-merge. Under five minutes for the PR loop is the target.
- **"Two teams want different React versions."** — Usually a symptom, not a requirement. If genuine, that is one of the few real arguments for splitting — and it costs you a shared design system.
- **"How do you migrate 200 call sites?"** — Codemod, land it in batches by owner, keep both paths working during the transition, and delete the old one on a dated deadline.
